title: The Crusades: Holy War and Holy Trade

cards.h: Holy war with a price tag
cards.b:
The Crusades lasted, on and off, from 1095 to the 1290s. They shaped how Europe and the Muslim world saw each other, and their memory is still used in politics today.

People went on Crusade for faith, for land, for money and for fame. Most of them were not thinking about the long-term effects. Those effects reached far beyond the Holy Land.

cards.h: A pope calls for a holy war
cards.b:
In November 1095 Pope Urban II spoke at Clermont in France. He asked knights to free the Christians of the East and take Jerusalem. Those who went and died, he promised, would have their sins forgiven.

A large crowd roared the answer, "God wills it." Preachers such as Peter the Hermit led a popular movement. Some of these groups attacked Jewish communities along the Rhine in 1096, a terrible episode that shows the violence the call could unleash.

The main crusader army reached Jerusalem in 1099 after a long march through Anatolia and Syria. It took the city in July after a short siege, and chroniclers describe a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish residents.

The crusaders set up states along the coast and inland: Jerusalem, Antioch, Edessa and Tripoli. Europeans called them the Outremer, or land beyond the sea. They lasted for almost two centuries.

cards.h: Usama ibn Munqidh and the Franks
cards.b:
Usama ibn Munqidh (1095–1188)

A Syrian noble and warrior, Usama wrote a memoir called Kitab al-I'tibar (The Book of Contemplation). He describes Frankish knights as rough and proud, but he also records friendships and cases where Franks showed him courtesy.

His book reminds us that the Crusades were lived by ordinary people on both sides. It was not just one story of good against evil.
The Crusades were not one war. They were a long series of campaigns, sieges and truces, fought by armies that changed every few years.

In 1187 Saladin defeated the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin and then took Jerusalem. Europe was shocked, and the Third Crusade (1189–1192) was called to win it back.

Richard the Lionheart of England and Philip II of France led the army. Richard won some victories but never took Jerusalem. The Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 left the city in Muslim hands, though Christian pilgrims could visit it.

A famous story tells of thousands of children who marched to Jerusalem in 1212, only to be sold into slavery or to die on the way. It is one of the most haunting tales of the medieval world.

Historians argue about it. The sources are thin and written later. Some believe a real movement of young people happened, but the stories of mass child slavery look more like legend or moral warning. The debate is still open.

cards.h: The Fourth Crusade turns on Christians
cards.b:
In 1204 the Fourth Crusade was meant to attack Egypt. But the crusaders were deep in debt to Venice, which wanted its own gains. They ended up storming Constantinople, a Christian city.

The sack of Constantinople shocked the Byzantines. Treasures and relics were carried off to Venice and the West. A Latin empire ruled the city until 1261, and many Greeks never forgave the Latins for it.

Italian port cities like Venice and Genoa grew rich carrying crusaders and their supplies. They gained trading colonies in the eastern Mediterranean and new contacts with Arab and Byzantine merchants.

Historians argue whether the Crusades were mainly religious or mainly economic. The best answer is that faith, power and profit were tangled together. Crusading ideas also influenced later wars in Spain and the Baltic.

Saladin treated Jerusalem with more restraint than the crusaders had shown in 1099. He allowed Christians to stay and, according to later accounts, he ransomed many prisoners at a low price.

His reputation grew in Europe as well. Medieval writers made him into a model of chivalry, and his story became a favourite among later storytellers and poets.

The last crusader stronghold, Acre, fell to the Mamluks in 1291. The crusading states were gone, but the memory of the Crusades lived on in art, literature and political language.

In the modern world, the word "crusade" is used in political speeches on both sides. Historians now try to tell the story from many viewpoints, including those of Muslims, Byzantines and local Christians.

In 1192 Muhammad of Ghor defeated the Rajput ruler Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain, near Delhi. The victory opened the way for Turkish and Afghan rulers to set up a sultanate in Delhi.

Qutb-ud-din Aibak, one of Muhammad's generals, became the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Across the world, the same century saw holy wars and new states spreading in different directions.

Five things to remember
  1. Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095.
  2. The crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099.
  3. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.
  4. The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204.
  5. Acre fell in 1291, ending the crusader states.
Think about it
  • Were the Crusades a religious war, an economic one, or both?
  • Why do Crusade stories still stir strong feelings today?
